dimensions.definition: Specific, directional (verbal) predictions the study set to test out (usually stated in the Introduction [frequently at the end of the introduction] or right before the introduction of a new study), including effects which are confirmatory vs. exploratory. Relevant keywords: 'expect(ed)', 'predict(ed)', or 'hypothesise(d)'. for primary hypotheses: 'key', 'leading', 'main', 'major', 'primary', or 'principal'. for secondary hypotheses: 'additional', 'auxiliary', 'minor', or 'secondary'.
Where the data will be / was obtained, and the processes therein. For example, a student sample, online (e.g., m-turk, prolific), the community, an existing archival dataset, etc.

Inclusion criteria specify how subjects (or units of analysis otherwise specified) are selected for eligibility in the study.
Exclusion criteria specify how data exclusions are determined (e.g., how will outliers be determined? Will awareness checks be implemented?).
The precise number of participants that the researchers intend to sample or a range, minimum, or maximum. This can also include a stopping rule if one is specified.
Variables that are experimentally manipulated, that is, the experimenter controlled the level / treatment that participants received.
Variables that are observed/ recorded in a study. This can include outcome measures, as well as any measured predictors or covariates.
The statistical tests that are used to analyse the data, based on the manipulated and measured variables, to address the research questions and hypotheses.
Approaches to processing data from one form, structure, or scale to another to prepare it for analysis (e.g., log transforming, centering, or recoding the data).
Information about how missing data will be handled in the processing and analysis of the study.

All explicitly stated conditions, characteristics, or thresholds that must be satisfied for a participant or study unit (e.g., individual, cluster, site) to be enrolled in the study. This includes required demographic characteristics (e.g., age range, sex/gender, pregnancy/menopausal status), diagnosis or target condition (including staging, severity, symptom duration, biomarker status), clinical status (e.g., performance status, treatment-naïve status), prior or current treatments that are required or permitted, contextual factors (e.g., recruitment setting, healthcare setting, geography), and other positive requirements (e.g., language proficiency, ability to comply with study procedures, capacity to consent, access to required technology or devices), typically expressed using terms such as “must have,” “must meet,” “only participants with,” or “eligible if.” Commonly appears as bullet points or prose under headings such as “Inclusion criteria,” “Eligibility criteria,” or “Participants” in trial registries, protocols, and manuscripts.

All explicitly stated conditions or characteristics that disqualify a participant from enrollment or continued participation in the study. This includes safety-related exclusions (e.g., contraindications, relevant comorbidities, allergies, pregnancy where specified as exclusion, severe organ dysfunction), protocol- or confounding-related exclusions (e.g., concurrent trial participation, use of prohibited concomitant treatments, prior exposure to the study intervention beyond allowed limits), feasibility-related exclusions (e.g., inability or unwillingness to adhere to required visits, procedures, or follow-up), and history or condition-based exclusions indicated by phrases such as “must not,” “excluded if,” “no history of,” or “not eligible if.” Commonly appears under “Exclusion criteria” or within “Eligibility”/“Participants” sections in trial registries, protocols, and manuscripts.

The detailed specification of each study arm, including both experimental and comparator arms. This encompasses the name or identity of the intervention (e.g., drug, biologic, device, surgical procedure, behavioural or psychological program, digital/app-based intervention), the dose or intensity (e.g., strength, amount, frequency, duration of sessions), route or mode of administration (e.g., oral, IV, subcutaneous, inhaled, implanted, online, in-person, telephone), schedule and timing (including dosing schedules, titration, tapering, timing relative to baseline or randomisation), planned duration of administration, and a clear description of the control or comparator condition, such as placebo (including route and appearance), sham procedure, active control (with its own dose and schedule), or usual/standard care (with defining elements). It also includes any mandated co-interventions (e.g., background therapy) and any explicitly prohibited concomitant treatments. Commonly appears under headings such as “Interventions,” “Study treatments,” “Arm description,” “Trial arms,” or “Treatment protocol.”

The specific identifier(s) associated with ethical approval of the study, including ethics committee/IRB/REC/REB approval numbers, protocol codes linked to ethics approval, national or institutional reference numbers, and identifiers for substantial amendments where explicitly reported. These identifiers are typically presented in sections or statements labelled “Ethics approval,” “Ethical considerations,” “IRB (Institutional Review Board) approval,” or similar, and may appear in trial registries, protocols, and manuscripts.

The official name(s) of the ethics body or bodies responsible for reviewing and approving the study, such as Institutional Review Boards (IRBs), Research Ethics Committees (RECs), Research Ethics Boards (REBs), hospital or university ethics committees, and national or regional competent authorities performing ethics review. Names often include the institution and country or region (e.g., “University X Research Ethics Committee, Country Y”) and are typically reported in ethics-related sections or statements in trial registries, protocols, and manuscripts.

The calendar date on which ethics approval was granted for the primary study protocol, and, where explicitly reported, the dates on which major amendments were approved. Dates may be presented in full (e.g., “15 March 2022”) or in partial formats (e.g., month/year) and are usually mentioned alongside the ethics committee name or approval number in sections titled “Ethics approval,” “Ethical considerations,” or similar in trial registries, protocols, and manuscripts.

The numerical specification of the number of participants associated with the study, including planned or target total sample size, planned or target per-arm sample size (where reported), and actual numbers enrolled, randomized, allocated, or analyzed, overall and by arm (where reported). Expressions may include phrases such as “target sample size,” “planned enrollment,” “anticipated enrollment,” “a total of N participants,” “we aimed to recruit,” or “N participants were randomized/analyzed,” and typically appear in “Sample size,” “Methods,” “Participants,” “Study design,” “Statistical methods,” enrollment fields, or CONSORT-style flow diagrams.

The planned or actual date on which enrollment of the first participant began. This may be expressed as an exact date (e.g., “Recruitment started on 01 June 2021”) or a less specific time reference (e.g., “Recruitment commenced in June 2021”) and is commonly found in fields or text labelled “Study start date,” “Date of first enrollment,” “Recruitment,” or within “Methods” and “Study design” sections in trial registries, protocols, and manuscripts.

All outcome measures explicitly designated as “primary,” “main,” or “primary endpoint(s)” that define the principal endpoints of interest for evaluating the intervention. A well-specified primary outcome typically includes: (a) the outcome domain or construct (e.g., overall survival, hospitalization, pain, HbA1c, depression severity), (b) the measurement instrument or operational definition (e.g., named clinical scale, laboratory test, imaging modality, diagnostic or response criteria, event definition algorithm), (c) the metric or scale (e.g., absolute value, change from baseline, proportion meeting a threshold, time-to-event, rate, composite index, including units where applicable), and (d) the assessment timepoint(s) (e.g., at 12 weeks, day 28, at discharge, 6 months post-randomisation). Such information is typically reported in “Primary outcome(s)” or “Endpoints” fields, “Outcomes” or “Endpoints” sections, abstracts, and statistical analysis descriptions. Some primary outcomes may be composites of other primary or secondary outcomes.

All outcome measures explicitly labelled as “secondary,” “key secondary,” or similar that are intended to provide supportive, exploratory, mechanistic, or safety-related information beyond the primary endpoints. A well-specified secondary outcome similarly includes: (a) the outcome domain or construct, (b) the measurement instrument or operational definition, (c) the metric or scale, and (d) the assessment timepoint(s). These outcomes may include safety endpoints, adverse events, laboratory parameters, quality of life, functional status, biomarker changes, intermediate clinical outcomes, or subgroup-specific effects, and are typically documented in “Secondary outcome(s)” fields and “Secondary outcomes” or “Endpoints” sections. Some secondary outcomes may be composites of other primary or secondary outcomes.

The described method used to generate and implement the allocation of participants or clusters to study arms. This includes the sequence generation approach (e.g., computer-generated random numbers, random-number tables, permuted block randomisation with or without specified block sizes, stratified randomisation by site or baseline characteristics, minimiz(s)ation or dynamic allocation procedures), the allocation ratio between arms (e.g., 1:1, 2:1, 3:1:1), and, where described in the same context, the allocation concealment mechanism (e.g., central randomisation, secure web- or telephone-based systems such as IWRS/IVRS, pharmacy-controlled allocation, sealed opaque sequentially numbered envelopes). Common textual indicators include phrases such as “participants were randomiz(s)ed using…,” “random sequence generated by…,” “block size…,” “stratified by…,” and “allocation was concealed using…,” and this information typically appears in “Randomiz(s)ation,” “Study design,” or “Methods” sections and corresponding fields in trial documentation.

The central question or claim the study is designed to address and the specific predictions it sets out to test, as stated prior to data collection. This includes the direction of each predicted effect where applicable, the distinction between confirmatory (pre-specified, hypothesis-testing) and exploratory (hypothesis-generating) analyses, and any primary versus secondary hypotheses. Note whether the questions and predictions tested in the paper match those registered in the pre-analysis plan, and whether any were added, dropped, or reframed after seeing the data. Typically stated in the introduction, 'Research questions', 'Hypotheses', or a pre-analysis-plan summary.

The data underlying the analysis and how the analysis sample is built. This includes the dataset(s) or data source (e.g., administrative records, survey, experiment, panel, archival/secondary data), the unit of observation (individual, household, firm, region, country-year), the time period and geographic scope, and the sample-construction rules (inclusion/exclusion filters, trimming, the population frame, and for primary data the collection procedure and target sample). Note any difference between the planned sample and the realised analysis sample. Typically reported in 'Data', 'Sample', 'Setting', or the early 'Methods'/'Empirical strategy' sections.

The research design used to identify the effect of interest and the assumptions it relies on. This includes the design type (randomised controlled trial / field experiment, instrumental variables, difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity, event study, synthetic control, matching, panel/fixed-effects, or a structural model), the source of identifying variation, the unit or level of randomisation or treatment assignment, and the key identifying assumptions (e.g., exclusion restriction and instrument relevance, parallel trends, continuity at the threshold, conditional independence/selection on observables). Note whether the strategy and assumptions in the paper match the pre-specified design. Typically reported in 'Empirical strategy', 'Identification', 'Research design', or 'Methods'.

The treatment or causal variable of interest and the comparison against which its effect is estimated. For experiments this includes the treatment arm(s) and intervention content (what was delivered, dose/intensity, delivery mode, timing, and duration), the control or comparison arm, the randomisation ratio, and expected take-up/compliance. For observational designs this includes the definition of the treatment/exposure variable, any instrument(s) and the exclusion restriction invoked, and the comparison group or counterfactual (e.g., not-yet-treated units, below-threshold units). Note any mandated co-interventions or excluded conditions. Typically reported in 'Intervention', 'Treatment', 'Experimental design', or 'Empirical strategy'.

The dependent variables used to evaluate the effect, distinguishing primary from secondary outcomes. A well-specified outcome includes (a) the construct or domain (e.g., earnings, employment, test scores, consumption, take-up), (b) the operational definition and data source, (c) how it is constructed and scaled (level, log, change, share, standardised z-score, an index of several measures, winsorised/top-coded), and (d) the measurement timing or horizon. Note any pre-specified primary outcome or index, whether the paper's primary outcome matches the registered one, and any outcomes reported but not pre-specified (or vice versa). Typically reported in 'Outcomes', 'Variables', 'Measurement', or the pre-analysis plan.

The basis for the study's statistical precision, as planned. This includes the target sample size (overall and per arm or cell), any a priori power calculation or minimum detectable effect (MDE), and the assumptions behind it (assumed effect size, baseline variance, significance level and power, intra-cluster correlation and number of clusters for clustered designs, and expected take-up/attrition). Note whether the realised sample and design achieve the planned precision and whether the power analysis was pre-specified. Typically reported in 'Power', 'Sample size', 'Experimental design', or the pre-analysis plan; it is often absent in observational work, which is itself worth noting.

The estimating equation(s) and model used to obtain the main results, as pre-specified. This includes the estimator (e.g., OLS, 2SLS/IV, logit/probit, Poisson, maximum likelihood, GMM, local polynomial), the exact specification (outcome and treatment variables, control variables/covariates, fixed effects, interaction terms, functional form, and any weighting), the level of aggregation, and how the treatment-effect parameter is defined (intention-to-treat versus treatment-on-the-treated/LATE). Note any divergence between the planned and reported specification, including added or dropped controls or a changed functional form. Typically reported in 'Empirical strategy', 'Estimation', 'Specification', or 'Methods'.

How statistical inference is conducted and how multiple comparisons are handled, as planned. This includes the method for computing standard errors and the level of clustering (e.g., heteroskedasticity-robust, cluster-robust at a stated level, HAC/Newey-West, wild-cluster bootstrap, randomisation/permutation inference), and the approach to multiple-hypothesis testing across outcomes, subgroups, or treatment arms (e.g., pre-specified outcome families, summary indices, family-wise error-rate or false-discovery-rate corrections, sharpened q-values). Note whether the inference and corrections in the paper match what was pre-specified. Typically reported in 'Inference', 'Standard errors', 'Statistical analysis', or notes to the main tables.

Pre-specified analyses of how the effect varies across units or contexts. This includes the subgroups or moderators to be examined (e.g., by sex, age, baseline status, region, treatment intensity), the dimensions of treatment-effect heterogeneity of interest, and how these will be tested (interaction terms, split samples, or pre-specified machine-learning/causal-forest approaches), including any correction for the additional tests. Note whether the heterogeneity analyses in the paper were pre-registered or appear exploratory, and whether subgroups were added or dropped. Typically reported in 'Heterogeneity', 'Subgroup analysis', or the pre-analysis plan.

How the study handles incomplete data and shows that results are not artefacts of analytic choices, as planned. This includes the treatment of attrition and non-response (e.g., differential-attrition tests, bounds such as Lee bounds, inverse-probability weighting), the handling of missing values and outliers (imputation, winsorising, trimming), and the set of pre-specified robustness and sensitivity checks (alternative specifications, alternative samples or RDD bandwidths, placebo/falsification tests, controlling for additional covariates). Note any divergence between planned and reported handling, and any robustness checks added after the fact. Typically reported in 'Robustness', 'Sensitivity analysis', 'Attrition', or appendices.

Whether the study is described as exploratory (hypothesis-generating, with outcomes and analyses not fully pre-specified) or confirmatory (hypothesis-testing, with pre-specified predictions, outcomes, and analyses), and whether this designation is consistent between the protocol/preregistration and the publication. Confirmatory work states specific predictions before data collection and tests them with pre-specified analyses; exploratory work investigates patterns without prespecified hypotheses. Look for explicit statements (e.g., 'this study was exploratory/confirmatory', 'hypothesis-generating', 'pre-specified primary analysis') and for whether the paper retrospectively reframes exploratory analyses as confirmatory (or vice versa). Commonly indicated in the title, abstract, 'Study design', or 'Statistical analysis' sections.

The total number of animals planned for the study, the sum across all experimental and control groups as stated in the protocol, and, where reported, the number of animals actually used, randomised, or analysed overall. May be described as total sample size, number of animals, total N, planned cohort size, or the estimated number of animals declared to an ethics or animal-welfare body. The experimental unit (animal, litter, cage, or cohort) should be considered, and discrepancies may arise from attrition, mortality, humane endpoints, or exclusions; note any difference between the planned total and the number ultimately analysed. Typically reported in 'Animals', 'Sample size', 'Methods', ethics/licence sections, or a study-flow diagram.

The planned number of animals allocated to each experimental and control group (group size, per-group sample size, n per arm/condition) as stated in the protocol, and, where reported, the actual numbers per group. This is often justified by an a priori power or sample-size calculation (assumed effect size, variability, alpha, power) or by a resource-equation/3Rs rationale. Note any divergence between planned and realised group sizes and whether the experimental unit is the individual animal or a higher-level unit (litter, cage). Typically reported in 'Animals', 'Sample size', 'Experimental design', or 'Statistical methods' sections, or in figure legends.

The specific intervention(s) planned and the control or comparator condition against which they are assessed. For the intervention this includes its identity (e.g., compound/drug, biologic, genetic or surgical manipulation, dietary or behavioural manipulation, device), the dose or intensity (amount, concentration, frequency), the route or mode of administration (e.g., oral gavage, intraperitoneal, intravenous, subcutaneous, inhaled, surgical), and the schedule, timing, and planned duration of administration. For the control this includes the comparator condition (e.g., vehicle, sham surgery, untreated, wild-type or littermate control, naive animals) specified with the same level of detail (route, volume, timing). It also includes any mandated co-interventions and explicitly prohibited concomitant treatments. Typically reported under 'Interventions', 'Treatments', 'Experimental groups', 'Study design', or 'Methods'.

Methods planned to reduce the risk of bias in conducting and analysing the study. This includes randomisation of animals (or higher-level units) to groups and the sequence-generation method (e.g., computer-generated random numbers, block or stratified randomisation), allocation concealment, and blinding/masking of those administering interventions, caring for animals, assessing outcomes, and analysing data. It also covers other bias-mitigation steps such as pre-specified inclusion/exclusion rules for animals or data points, randomised order of treatment and measurement, and steps to control for cage, litter, batch, or experimenter effects. Note whether each measure is stated as planned and whether the paper reports it as implemented. Commonly reported in 'Randomisation', 'Blinding', 'Experimental design', or 'Methods' sections (aligned with ARRIVE 2.0 items).

All outcome measures explicitly designated as primary, main, or the principal endpoint(s) used to evaluate the intervention. A well-specified primary outcome includes (a) the outcome domain or construct (e.g., tumour volume, infarct size, lesion area, survival, a behavioural readout, a physiological or molecular marker), (b) the measurement instrument or operational definition (e.g., named assay, imaging modality, behavioural test, histological scoring method), (c) the metric or scale (e.g., absolute value, change from baseline, proportion meeting a threshold, time-to-event, including units), and (d) the assessment timepoint(s) (e.g., at day 14, 6 weeks post-induction, terminal). Note whether the primary outcome named in the paper matches the one pre-specified in the protocol. Typically reported in 'Primary outcome', 'Outcomes', 'Endpoints', or the statistical-analysis description. Some primary outcomes may be composites of other outcomes.

All outcome measures explicitly labelled as secondary, additional, or exploratory that provide supportive, mechanistic, or safety/welfare-related information beyond the primary endpoint. A well-specified secondary outcome similarly includes (a) the outcome domain or construct, (b) the measurement instrument or operational definition, (c) the metric or scale, and (d) the assessment timepoint(s). These may include additional behavioural, physiological, biochemical, histological, or molecular measures, adverse events or tolerability/welfare indicators, and subgroup or time-course analyses. Note any secondary outcomes reported in the paper that were not pre-specified, or pre-specified ones not reported. Typically reported in 'Secondary outcomes', 'Outcomes', or 'Endpoints' sections.

The statistical methods planned to test each hypothesis or estimate each effect, as specified before data collection. This includes the specific tests or models (e.g., t-test, ANOVA, mixed-effects/multilevel models, survival analysis, regression), the experimental unit used for analysis (animal, litter, cage), the handling of nested or repeated-measures data, covariates and factors included, planned corrections for multiple comparisons, the criterion for statistical significance, and rules for handling missing data, outliers, and excluded animals. Note any divergence between the planned analysis and the analysis reported, including added, removed, or changed tests. Typically reported in 'Statistical analysis', 'Data analysis', or 'Methods' sections.

The specific predictions the study set out to test, as stated prior to data collection, including their direction (e.g., which group is expected to differ and in which direction) and whether each is designated confirmatory or exploratory. A well-specified hypothesis links a predicted effect to the intervention and the primary outcome. Note whether the hypotheses tested in the paper match those registered in direction and operationalisation, and whether any predictions appear to have been added, dropped, or reversed after seeing the data. Typically reported in the introduction, 'Objectives/Aims', 'Hypotheses', or 'Study design' sections.
Specific predictions or expectations the study set out to test, including their status as confirmatory or exploratory, their direction, and any preregistered null or equivalence expectations.

Where and from whom the data come: target population, sampling frame, survey firm or panel provider, country or case selection, recruitment channels, and any registered data-collection window or waves.

The experimental or quasi-experimental interventions: treatment and control conditions, vignettes, framing or information treatments, conjoint attributes and levels, and the randomisation procedure and unit of assignment.

The outcome variables and how they are measured: question wording, scales, indices and how they are constructed, behavioural measures, coding schemes, and the designation of primary versus secondary outcomes.

The quantity to be estimated (e.g. average treatment effect, conditional effects, intention-to-treat) and the estimation strategy: estimator, model form, covariate set, fixed effects, standard-error clustering or robust corrections, and any registered hierarchy of specifications.
The planned and achieved number of observations, power analysis or minimum-detectable-effect calculations, and any stopping or data-collection rules.

Who is included or excluded and on what registered criteria: eligibility rules, attention or comprehension screeners, speeders, duplicate or fraudulent responses, and whether exclusions are applied pre- or post-treatment.
Preregistered moderators, interaction terms, and subgroup analyses, including which are confirmatory versus exploratory and any registered expectations about heterogeneous effects.
How dropout, nonresponse, and missing values are handled: registered rules for imputation or exclusion, checks for differential attrition across conditions, and item-nonresponse handling.
Whether and how survey weights, post-stratification, or raking are applied, and any registered corrections for multiple comparisons across outcomes, specifications, or subgroups.

rr_addons.definition: Outcome-neutral criteria specified at Stage 1 that determine whether the data can test the hypotheses regardless of results: data-quality thresholds, manipulation checks, positive and negative controls, and baseline or randomisation checks — and whether Stage 2 reports them and whether they were satisfied.

Whether the Stage 1 text that carries forward into Stage 2 (introduction, hypotheses, methods, analysis plan) is preserved as written, apart from licensed changes. The excerpts below are the most-changed carried-forward passages, identified by a mechanical text comparison of the two manuscripts, each shown as the Stage 1 wording followed by its Stage 2 counterpart.

dimensions.definition: Whether each hypothesis is stated precisely enough to be falsifiable: every prediction associated with each hypothesis is precisely defined — the predicted relationship is directional (or explicitly non-directional), names the specific variables involved, and states the population or conditions it applies to. A hypothesis may bundle several predictions, provided each individual prediction meets this standard.

dimensions.dimension: Sample size or other stopping rules
dimensions.definition: Whether the registration pre-specifies the stopping rule for data collection and the criteria that define the final sample size for the study — that is, whether it is unambiguously defined what size of sample will be involved in the data analysis. Only analytical flexibility related to the stopping rule is at issue here: a justification of the sample-size target (e.g. via power analysis) is NOT required, and its absence must not count against the registration, as long as the stopping rule is concrete and the size of the sample that will enter the data analysis is unambiguously defined. Likewise, recruitment details (channels, panel provider, compensation, setting) are not required by this dimension. A common problem related to the preregistration of stopping rules is ambiguity about whether a prespecified target sample size will trigger the stopping of data collection before or after accounting for exclusions, dropouts, or other types of missing data. A statement like "the target sample size will be 150 participants" alone is inadequate and would require revision.

This aspect covers assumptions of specific statistical tests that are involved in the study, and the actions proposed in the event of violation of these assumptions. Importantly, the evaluation should not include flexibility related to inference criteria or the statistical model specifications, because they are part of a different aspect of the preregistration according to this taxonomy. The evaluation should only focus on researcher degrees of freedom related to assumption checks and assumption violation handling procedures. Even though outliers and missing data are included in the assumptions of some statistical models, do not include these aspects in the evaluation of this dimension, because there is another evaluation dimension specifically addressing outliers and missing data. Common problems related to this aspect of the preregistration include only addressing one or a few assumptions while leaving other important assumptions unchecked, or only addressing the assumptions of one test but not all tests in the study. Other common issues include only mentioning assumption checking, but not specifying the method of the assumption check, or how a potential violation will be handled. In these cases revision of the preregistration might be required.

dimensions.dimension: Exclusion of observations, handling outliers and missing data
dimensions.definition: This aspect covers analytical degrees of freedom related to which specific observations to include in the analysis and how to handle missing data. Specifically, it focuses on decisions applied at the "row level" of a wide-format dataset, such as those involving participants, trials, or sessions. It includes, but is not limited to, data exclusion criteria, handling of missing or incomplete data, treatment of outliers, and attrition or dropout handling. For example, these decisions may involve excluding participants who fail attention or other data quality checks, excluding trials with response times below or above a prespecified threshold, determining whether participants with incomplete task completion are retained or excluded, or deciding how participants who drop out partway through the study are treated in the analysis. They may also involve decisions related to how missing observations are handled (e.g. omitted or replaced) in the analysis, or how extreme cases are handled (e.g. omitted, transformed, or replaced). Any flexibility in determining which observations are included or excluded from the analysis, or how missing, incomplete, or extreme values are handled, should be explicitly specified in the preregistration. Because these decisions can often be implemented in multiple defensible ways, the preregistration should clearly constrain these choices to reduce analytical flexibility and researcher degrees of freedom. Common problems related to this aspect include that handling of missing data and/or extreme cases is not specified, or that this is mentioned in the preregistration but it is not specific enough. If the preregistered procedure allows for alternative decisions that could be selectively applied to influence which observations are entered into the primary analyses, or which observations should be transformed or replaced over others, even while technically adhering to the preregistration, then the preregistration is insufficient and should be revised.

This aspect covers the selection and manipulation of variables or scales to represent constructs that play a role in the main hypotheses of the study — typically as independent variables, dependent variables, outcomes, or covariates. It refers to decisions applied at the "column level" of a wide-format dataset (affecting whole variables rather than individual observations). In many research studies, the construct of interest is measured using multiple scales, instruments, or operationalisations, and it needs to be specified which of the collected or computed variables will be used to test the hypotheses. In other situations, the gathered raw data is not directly used to test the hypothesis; rather, the raw data is combined, aggregated, transformed, or otherwise processed to better resemble the construct of interest. Common issues include: the construct of interest is measured using multiple scales, instruments, or operationalisations, but the preregistration fails to specify which of these will be used in the primary analyses (e.g. the authors note that "pain level will be predicted by the procedure used" but multiple pain measures are used and it is not clear which one will be entered into the model, or how these will be combined into a single "pain level"); vague statements such as "we will use the most reliable measure" or "the variable that shows strongest effects," which leave room for post hoc selection, or ambiguity about whether control variables are used. Even if all candidate measures are listed, if the criteria for choosing among them are not fully specified prior to data analysis, the preregistration allows for potentially biasing flexibility. In other cases, the preprocessing or computation procedure used to derive the variables entered into the primary analysis is not clearly specified (e.g. "transformed variables will be used", or "after preprocessing according to standards in the literature, spectral density will be computed"), or the authors note that the total score of a scale will be used but the scale does not conventionally yield a total score (subscales are interpreted individually), so it is unclear how that score will be computed. Only consider degrees of freedom related to which variables are chosen for analysis and how they are generated or computed — not how these variables are analysed in a statistical model or how results are interpreted (which are part of other dimensions). Evaluate whether the preregistration defines the exact variables or measurement instruments that will be used for each key construct in the confirmatory analysis and, if a variable in the analysis is produced by preprocessing or manipulation, whether the procedures for that computation are specified clearly. If multiple operationalisations are possible even after following the preregistration exactly, and this flexibility introduces a risk of bias, the preregistration needs to be revised.

This aspect includes manipulation checks, outcome-neutral checks, or tests of intervention fidelity. In experimental studies these include testing whether the experimental manipulation worked as intended. In observational studies they might include parallel measurements to replicate an established fact, thus confirming that the design or instrumentation is sufficiently sensitive to detect the existence of the phenomenon that forms the main focus of the research. There are multiple ways in which manipulation checks can be conducted for any given study, and the consequence of a failed test (finding that implementing the experimental manipulation was unsuccessful) can also be wide-ranging, from a simple note in the limitations section to exclusion of entire conditions or subgroups, or the dismissal of the findings of a study. Manipulation checks are commonly not registered at all, or if they are, the procedure is not specified enough — including how the check is done, how a decision based on the check is made — or the consequence of possible findings of the checks can be non- or ill-defined. Evaluate whether there are degrees of freedom left that can be used opportunistically to change the conclusions of the research even if the manipulation check procedure described in the registration is followed exactly. If so, the preregistration is inadequate and should be revised. Distinguish manipulation checks from general data-quality or attention checks. Procedures that only verify that participants can perceive the stimuli, are paying attention, or are responding seriously — e.g. audio or sound checks, attention-check items, comprehension screeners, catch trials, duplicate-response checks, or speeding checks — are NOT manipulation checks: they verify data quality rather than whether the manipulation produced its intended effect, and they are assessed under the exclusion-of-observations dimension instead. A procedure counts under this dimension only if it measures whether the manipulated variable had its intended proximal effect (e.g. whether participants in a negative-interaction condition actually perceived the interaction as negative, whether an emotion induction shifted the target emotion, or whether intervention delivery met fidelity criteria). If the registration contains only data-quality checks and no such test, judge this dimension "not present".

This aspect covers the specification of the statistical models and methods that will be used to analyse the data. This includes, but is not limited to, the type of model (e.g., linear regression, mixed-effects model, ANOVA) and the structure of the model (e.g., fixed vs. random effects, nesting, covariates). Importantly, it should be clearly defined what statistical technique will be applied to test each specific hypothesis or research question. The evaluation should focus solely on the specification of the statistical method itself, including model architecture, without evaluating how statistical significance or conclusions will be derived from the model output — those aspects are handled in a separate dimension called Inference, and should not be considered in this evaluation. Common problems related to this aspect include ambiguity or underspecification about which statistical method will be used to analyse which key hypotheses, or lack of detail about model structure, such as incomplete specification of whether multiple predictors will be tested in the same or in separate models. Evaluate whether the statistical methods are described precisely enough that the exact analysis pipeline could be reconstructed by a third party, and whether any remaining analytical flexibility could be exploited to bias the results. If implementing the preregistered plan exactly would still allow for meaningful researcher degrees of freedom in model selection or specification, then the preregistration is inadequate and should be revised.

This aspect covers how inferences will be drawn from the statistical analyses, including decision rules for interpreting results. This includes criteria for statistical significance (e.g., α levels), correction for multiple comparisons, the use of confidence intervals, Bayes factors, or any other inferential threshold. Importantly, this dimension is distinct from Statistical method specification, which concerns the model itself, and from Variable specification and preprocessing, which concerns which variables are analysed. Common problems include vague or missing inferential criteria (e.g. whether one- or two-sided tests will be used), unspecified procedures for multiple comparisons, or failure to define thresholds for interpretation. If multivariate or other complex models are proposed, or if multiple models are proposed for testing the hypothesis, much more detail might be required to limit freedom in inference. It is also common that multiple analyses are proposed for a single hypothesis, or that multiple estimates or significance tests are returned by a single model, but it is not specified how exactly these different results will contribute to the final inference about the hypothesis. If the preregistration allows flexibility in interpreting results, revision is likely needed.

Whether each objective or hypothesis is stated precisely enough to be falsifiable: every prediction associated with each objective is precisely defined — it names the intervention and comparator, the population it applies to, and the direction of the anticipated effect (or is explicitly framed as non-directional or estimation-only, e.g. superiority, non-inferiority, or equivalence with the framing stated). An objective may bundle several predictions, provided each individual prediction meets this standard.

Whether every intervention arm and comparator is fully operationalised: the intervention's components, dose, schedule, duration, and route or format of delivery are stated; the comparator (e.g. placebo, active control, usual care) is described to the same standard; the allocation method (randomisation procedure and allocation concealment) is specified; and blinding of participants, providers, and outcome assessors is stated.

Whether every outcome is fully operationalised: primary and secondary outcomes are designated; and for each outcome the measurement instrument or diagnostic criterion is named (including version where relevant), the analysis metric (e.g. change from baseline, endpoint value, time-to-event) and any aggregation method are stated, and the specific time point(s) of assessment are given.

dimensions.dimension: Sample size, stopping rules, and recruitment
dimensions.definition: Whether the registration specifies how many participants will be enrolled, when enrolment or the trial stops, and who will be recruited and how: the target sample size as an exact number or an unambiguous rule, with its statistical justification (e.g. the assumed effect size, alpha, power, and expected attrition); any planned interim analyses and early-stopping rules (for efficacy, futility, or harm); and the recruitment settings, sites, and enrolment procedures.

Whether inclusion and exclusion criteria are stated with explicit, checkable thresholds (e.g. age ranges, diagnostic criteria and the instruments used to apply them, disease-severity scores, comorbidity or concomitant-medication restrictions), precisely enough that an independent reader could determine any given patient's eligibility.

Whether the confirmatory analysis for each outcome is specified precisely enough to be reproduced without further decisions: the statistical model or test is named; the analysis population is defined (e.g. intention-to-treat, per-protocol, safety set); covariates or stratification factors and their roles are listed; and any model-selection, transformation, or assumption-handling steps are decided in advance rather than left open. (Decision thresholds such as the alpha level and test sidedness are assessed under the inference criteria dimension.)

Whether the registration states how missing data, dropouts, and protocol deviations will be handled in the analysis: the method (e.g. multiple imputation, mixed models, complete-case analysis), any thresholds for retaining partial cases, planned sensitivity analyses for missingness assumptions, and how participants who discontinue or deviate from protocol are treated.

Whether the registration states in advance what result will count as success or failure for each outcome: the decision criterion (e.g. a p-value threshold and test sidedness, a confidence-interval or non-inferiority margin, a Bayes factor bound), the alpha level where applicable, corrections for multiplicity across outcomes, arms, or interim looks, and how conflicting or partial patterns of results will be interpreted.

Whether the registration clearly separates confirmatory from exploratory elements: which outcomes and analyses are confirmatory commitments versus exploratory or hypothesis-generating; and whether the trial's status at registration (e.g. enrolment not yet begun, data not yet collected or accessed) is stated.
